gap: No result ChatGPT got states that Anker's own footnote only promises the A2687's full single-port output on US 100–130 V mains 'for at least 1 hour' at 77°F, with no derating only on 220–240 V; it also publishes no fixed multi-port split, so the '100 + 60 W' every rival gives for the Anker is not an Anker figure.
standout_why: Compared against itechguides.com (cited), the Notebookcheck news and review pages (cited), the anker.com A2687 page and service.anker.com spec page (cited) and our own dealectric.com page. itechguides gives no input ratings, no splits and no derating, and it compares the 4-port UGREEN. Notebookcheck covers only the UGREEN. On anker.com the 1-hour limit sits in footnote 1 and none of ChatGPT's answers repeated it. ChatGPT's tables and our page both show 'Laptop + phone 100 + 60 W' for the Anker, but anker.com and service.anker.com list only '160W Max' for two or three ports. Our page has adamtalks.tech's throttle to about 110 W, a third-party measurement, but not Anker's own 1-hour rating. None of the pages says the UGREEN reviewers disagree about the C3 port (100 W vs 30 W).
decides: This backs the current pick (UGREEN for a desk, Anker for travel) and takes away part of Anker's case. The Anker's '140 W any port' is guaranteed for only one hour on US mains, and its multi-device split is set by the mode, not fixed. In its default profile How-To Geek saw about 50 W per device with three devices attached. For a 16-inch MacBook Pro charged at 140 W for long sessions in the US, neither charger publishes a sustained rating, so the Anker's speed lead is not documented. The extra $60 buys size, weight and app control, not sustained power. The page should replace '100 + 60 W' for the Anker with 'no fixed split: 160 W shared by mode'.

findings.label: Single-port full-output duration by mains voltage
findings.value: No derating on 220–240 V; at least 1 hour on 100–130 V (at 77°F)
findings.source_title: Anker Prime Charger (160W, 3 Ports, Smart Display) - Anker US
findings.note: Verbatim footnote 1: 'At 77°F, single-port charging runs without derating in 220 - 240V areas, and for at least 1 hour in 100 - 130V areas.' US mains is 120 V, so the US 140 W rating is a 1-hour minimum. ComputingForGeeks (Lorna Chepkoech, updated 2026-10-28) repeats only the 220–240 V half.

findings.label: Multi-port split as published
findings.value: Two ports: 160 W max; three ports: 160 W max. No per-port figures
findings.note: anker.com gives the same figures. The A2687 page names Standard, AI and Custom modes and says C1 can be prioritised, but publishes no fixed split for any mode. Dynamic power distribution works only in AI Mode 2.0 and reallocates power every 2 minutes. Dual-Laptop Mode needs the app over Bluetooth.

findings.label: Single-port max: headline vs spec table
findings.value: Headline 140 W; spec table 150 W (28 V × 5.36 A), only when recharging an Anker Prime Power Bank (26K, 300W) in AI Mode 2.0 with a cable that does not come with the charger
findings.source_title: Anker Prime Charger (160W, 3 Ports, Smart Display) - Anker US
findings.note: service.anker.com footnote: 'when used with some Anker products and in AI 2.0 charging mode, the charger can output 28V 5.36A, 150W max'. For general devices the maximum is 140 W (28 V × 5 A).

findings.label: Measured split, default profile, 3 devices
findings.value: About 50 W each (two Anker SOLIX C300 + Moto Edge+ 2023)
findings.source_title: Anker Prime Charger (160W, 3 Ports, Smart Display) Review - How-To Geek
findings.note: Bertel King, 2025-11-03: 'The default charging profile balanced the speeds between these three devices, allocating each around 50W.' His example of 80 W + 80 W for two MacBooks is not a measurement.

findings.label: Per-port maximums
findings.value: C1 140 W, C2 140 W, C3 100 W, C4 30 W, USB-A 22.5 W; 160 W total
findings.source_title: One charger for almost everything: 5-port Ugreen Nexode Pro 160W review - Notebookcheck
findings.note: This conflicts with The Gadgeteer (https://the-gadgeteer.com/?p=510229, read 2026-11-14), which says C3 and C4 'top out at 30W each'. UGREEN's own page would settle it but returned HTTP 429 every time I tried. Until then, show C3 as disputed.

findings.label: Laptop-port output vs number of devices
findings.value: 100 W with up to 3 devices connected; 65 W with 4 or 5
findings.source_title: Ugreen's new 5-port 160W charger with display launches in the US - Notebookcheck News
findings.note: Article text: one USB-C port provides 'a consistent 100W with up to three devices connected or 65W with four or five devices attached'. It does not say which port. This is a stated tier, which the Anker does not publish.

findings.label: Measured laptop-port output with 4 other devices, 1-hour test
findings.source_title: One charger for almost everything: 5-port Ugreen Nexode Pro 160W review - Notebookcheck
findings.note: This fits the 65 W tier for 4–5 devices. Notebookcheck says the display reads 1–2 W off: it showed 51 W where the FNB58 read about 49.5 W. Our page already has this number; no rival page does.

findings.label: Rated AC input
findings.source_title: Anker Prime Charger (160W, 3 Ports, Smart Display) - Anker US

findings.label: Size and weight, normalised
findings.value: Anker 65 × 52 × 35 mm (prongs excluded, stated), 220 g; UGREEN about 76.2 × 76.2 × 35.6 mm, about 360 g (Notebookcheck measured) or 353 g (The Gadgeteer)
